etymology: A borrowing from French jérémiade (Oxford English Dictionary), which the American Heritage Dictionary traces to Jérémie, Jeremiah, the prophet of the book of Lamentations. The OED’s earliest English evidence is from 1780, in the writing of Hannah More.
biblical_def: A jeremiad is a long, mournful complaint, a speech or writing that laments the state of things and warns of judgment to come. The word carries the prophet’s name. Jeremiah wept over Judah before the fall of Jerusalem: "Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!" (Jer 9:1). In Lamentations the ruined city speaks: "Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow" (Lam 1:12). English borrowed his name for any bitter lament. The Christian observation: a true jeremiad does not end in complaint. In the middle of Lamentations the prophet turns: "It is of the LORD’S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness" (Lam 3:22–23). Jeremiah grieved because he loved the people and feared God, and his grief led him to hope in God.
webster_summary: A long lament or prophecy of doom (OED earliest 1780), named for Jeremiah, the weeping prophet of Lamentations. A godly lament ends in the mercies that are new every morning (Lam 3:22–23).
webster_full: JEREMIAD, n. (from 1780, OED) A long, mournful complaint or lamentation; a speech or writing that bewails the times and foretells judgment. From French jérémiade, after Jérémie, Jeremiah (American Heritage Dictionary).
Scripture note: Jeremiah is called the weeping prophet for passages such as Jer 9:1 and the laments of Lamentations.
scriptures: Jer 9:1
Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!
Lam 1:12
Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow, which is done unto me, wherewith the LORD hath afflicted me in the day of his fierce anger.
Lam 3:22
It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
Lam 3:23
They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
corruption_summary: Modern use has shrunk the jeremiad to a mere rant. Jeremiah’s lament was grief for sin and judgment, and it was held under hope in God’s faithfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: Today jeremiad usually names a tirade: a long complaint about politics, culture, or the young. The speaker stands outside the trouble and scolds it. Jeremiah stood inside it. He wept for the slain of his own people (Jer 9:1), and he named their sin because he feared the God they had forsaken.

Scripture draws the line between two kinds of grief. "Godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation"; "the sorrow of the world worketh death" (2Co 7:10). A lament that never reaches repentance, or never turns to the mercies that are new every morning (Lam 3:22–23), is only complaint.
roots_lines: Jeremiah: the prophet of Judah’s last days, received by the church as the writer of Lamentations
French jérémiade: a lament in the manner of Jeremiah
1780: OED’s earliest English evidence, in the writing of Hannah More
usage: "The editorial was a jeremiad against the decline of the town."
Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? (Lam 1:12).
They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness. (Lam 3:23).

etymology: From the old English form of the name Magdalene. The American Heritage Dictionary gives it as an alteration of (Mary) Magdalene, who was often pictured as a tearful penitent. The Oxford English Dictionary records the noun maudlin from around 1300, in a text on St. Mary Magdalen, and the adjective from 1607, in Thomas Middleton.
biblical_def: Maudlin means weakly or tearfully sentimental, full of self-pity. The word is the name Magdalene worn down by English speech. Mary Magdalene was often pictured as a tearful penitent, and her name came to stand for weeping that has no end and no aim. Scripture tells her story another way. Christ had delivered her: she was the woman "out of whom went seven devils" (Luk 8:2). She did weep at the tomb: "Mary stood without at the sepulchre weeping" (Joh 20:11). But the risen Lord called her by name, "Mary," and she answered, "Rabboni" (Joh 20:16). Then she ran with the news: "Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord" (Joh 20:18). The Christian observation: her tears were real grief, and they did not last. The risen Christ turned her weeping into the first witness of the resurrection. Maudlin names the tears and leaves out the Lord who dried them.
webster_summary: Tearfully sentimental, self-pitying (OED adjective from 1607); worn down from Magdalene, long pictured weeping. Scripture shows her tears turned to witness at the empty tomb (Joh 20:11–18).
webster_full: MAUDLIN, a. (from 1607, OED) Weakly sentimental; tearful; given to self-pity. An alteration of (Mary) Magdalene, often depicted as a tearful penitent (American Heritage Dictionary).
Earlier noun: maudlin, the name Magdalene itself, recorded from around 1300 (OED).
scriptures: Luk 8:2
And certain women, which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils,
But Mary stood without at the sepulchre weeping: and as she wept, she stooped down, and looked into the sepulchre,
Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master.
Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had spoken these things unto her.
Psa 30:5
For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
corruption_summary: Maudlin remembers Magdalene only by her tears. Scripture remembers her as a delivered woman whose grief was turned to joy and witness by the risen Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: A maudlin man weeps over himself. His sorrow turns inward and stays there, and he enjoys it a little. That is the sorrow of the world, and it goes nowhere good (2Co 7:10). The name was borrowed from a woman whose story runs the other way.

Mary Magdalene wept because her Lord was dead and his body was gone. Her grief lasted until he spoke her name. "Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning" (Psa 30:5). The word kept her tears and dropped the morning.
roots_summary: Magdalene → Middle English maudlin (the name, c. 1300, OED) → adjective maudlin, tearfully sentimental (1607, OED).
roots_lines: Magdalene: of Magdala, the name Scripture gives Mary (Luk 8:2)
c. 1300: maudlin as the English form of the name, OED
1607: maudlin as an adjective for tearful sentiment, Thomas Middleton (OED)
usage: "By midnight the reunion had turned maudlin."
Mary stood without at the sepulchre weeping. (Joh 20:11).
Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning. (Psa 30:5).

pos: noun (one who will not believe without proof)
etymology: An English compound of doubting + the proper name Thomas (Oxford English Dictionary), after the apostle Thomas, who would not believe Christ was risen until he was shown proof (John 20:24–29; American Heritage Dictionary). The OED’s earliest evidence is from 1671, in the writing of William Annand, dean of Edinburgh.
biblical_def: A doubting Thomas is a person who refuses to believe a thing until he has seen proof for himself. The phrase comes from the apostle Thomas, who was absent when the risen Christ first appeared to the disciples. When they told him, "We have seen the Lord," he answered, "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails … I will not believe" (Joh 20:25). Eight days later the Lord came again and offered him the proof: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands … and be not faithless, but believing" (Joh 20:27). Thomas made one of the plainest confessions in the Gospels: "My Lord and my God" (Joh 20:28). The Christian observation: the phrase remembers Thomas for his doubt, but the Gospel ends his story with worship. Christ also spoke a blessing over every believer who would come after: "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed" (Joh 20:29).
webster_summary: One who will not believe without proof (OED earliest 1671), after the apostle Thomas (Joh 20:25). His doubt ended in confession, "My Lord and my God" (Joh 20:28).
webster_full: DOUBTING THOMAS, n. (from 1671, OED) A person who habitually doubts, or who will not believe without direct evidence. After the apostle Thomas (Joh 20:24–29).
Compare unbelief; Scripture sets the blessing on those who believe without sight (Joh 20:29).
scriptures: The other disciples therefore said unto him, We have seen the Lord. But he said unto them, Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.
Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.
Heb 11:1
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
corruption_summary: Modern use treats the doubting Thomas as the model of a healthy skeptic. In Scripture his doubt was rebuked, met by the risen Christ, and ended in worship.
corruption_paragraphs: Our age praises doubt as a virtue in itself, and some even claim Thomas as its patron. The text gives him no such praise. Christ called his refusal faithlessness: "be not faithless, but believing" (Joh 20:27). The testimony of the other apostles was enough, and Thomas had set it aside.

Christ was patient with him. He came again, showed his wounds, and brought Thomas to the confession "My Lord and my God" (Joh 20:28). The lesson is not that doubt is noble. Faith rests on the testimony God has given, "the evidence of things not seen" (Heb 11:1), and the Lord blesses the man who believes it.
roots_lines: Thomas: one of the twelve, called Didymus (Joh 20:24)
Joh 20:25: his refusal to believe without seeing the wounds
1671: OED’s earliest evidence for the phrase, William Annand
usage: "Even the doubting Thomases on the council came around after the inspection."
Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed. (Joh 20:29).

etymology: From the proper name Bedlem (Oxford English Dictionary), the Middle English form of Bethlehem, used of the Hospital of Saint Mary of Bethlehem, a London institution for the mentally ill (American Heritage Dictionary). The OED’s earliest evidence for the word is from 1418.
biblical_def: Bedlam means a scene of noisy uproar and confusion. The word is Bethlehem, worn down by English speech. A London hospital named for St Mary of Bethlehem took in the mentally ill, and its worn-down name came to mean any scene of uproar and confusion. That is a long way from the town Scripture names. Bethlehem is the city of David, where the prophet said the ruler of Israel would be born: "But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel" (Mic 5:2). There the angel announced, "unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord" (Luk 2:11), and the heavenly host sang "on earth peace" (Luk 2:14). The Christian observation: English took the name of the town where the Prince of Peace was born and made it a word for confusion. Scripture says the opposite of God: "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace" (1Co 14:33).
webster_summary: A scene of uproar and confusion; originally a madhouse (OED earliest 1418). The word is Bethlehem, worn down, from a London hospital named for St Mary of Bethlehem. In Scripture Bethlehem is the birthplace of the Prince of Peace (Mic 5:2; Luk 2:11).
webster_full: BEDLAM, n. (from 1418, OED) A place or scene of noisy uproar and confusion. From Middle English Bedlem, the Hospital of Saint Mary of Bethlehem in London (American Heritage Dictionary).
Scripture note: Bethlehem, the city of David, birthplace of Christ (Mic 5:2; Luk 2:11).
scriptures: Mic 5:2

But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
Luk 2:11
For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.
Luk 2:14
Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
corruption_summary: English turned the name of the town where the Prince of Peace was born into a byword for chaos. God is not the author of confusion, but of peace (1Co 14:33).
corruption_paragraphs: The change from Bethlehem to bedlam took centuries, and no one meant it as an insult to the town. Even so, it shows how easily holy names wear down in common speech until no one remembers what they meant.

Disorder comes from sin and not from God. When Paul set order in the worship at Corinth, he gave the reason: "God is not the author of confusion, but of peace" (1Co 14:33). The child born in Bethlehem came to bring that peace (Luk 2:14), and his people are meant to show it.
roots_summary: Bethlehem → Middle English Bedlem → the Hospital of St Mary of Bethlehem, London → bedlam, uproar (OED earliest 1418).
roots_lines: Bethlehem: the city of David, birthplace of Christ (Mic 5:2; Luk 2:11)
Bedlem: the Middle English spelling of the name
usage: "When the power went out, the cafeteria was bedlam."
Unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour. (Luk 2:11).
God is not the author of confusion, but of peace. (1Co 14:33).
